"Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," the SpaceX CEO said.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big.

The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower.

It was a huge moment for SpaceX, bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship.

"Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines."

The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage.

V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9, SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide.

This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027.

That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height."

So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall.

Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load. Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher thrust V4 engines.November 16, 2026

The original Starship Flight 15 mission plan called for a double chopsticks catch, with both Super Heavy and Ship coming back to the launch tower for recovery.

This would have been feasible, as the catches were scheduled a day apart: Super Heavy would land just 6.5 minutes after launch, while Ship would circle Earth for 22.5 hours, and deploy a batch of SpaceX's Starlink V3 internet satellites, before coming home. (Ship ended up delivering the satellites as planned.)

The twofer didn't happen, however; Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday as a result. But that wasn't a huge deal, as SpaceX had already pulled off Super Heavy catches on three previous Starship flights.

The Ship catch was unprecedented, because it's been a taller order. Ship returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter. SpaceX hadn't even tried the maneuver before Flight 15, so executing it was a very big deal.

"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's Ship-landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #746. The Mavericks Band Members ‘Saddened’ by Name Rights Lawsuit From Raul Malo’s Widow

Paul Deakin, Jerry Dale McFadden and Eddie Perez say Betty Malo has been paid handsomely for their current tour.

The remaining members of Americana band The Mavericks have responded to a lawsuit brought by the widow of their late frontman Raul Malo.

Drummer Paul Deakin, keyboardist Jerry Dale McFadden and guitarist Eddie Perez wrote in a social media statement on Wednesday (Nov. 18), “We were saddened to learn that Betty Malo filed a lawsuit against us.” Betty sued the trio last week, alleging they should be prohibited from performing as The Mavericks following her husband’s 2025 death from cancer.

The crux of Betty’s lawsuit is a clause in the Mavericks’ operating agreement stating that the band could only use that name so long as Raul was involved. She says the surviving members are now violating this by touring with guest singers as “The Mavericks & Friends.”

Attorneys for Deakin, McFadden and Perez claim they amended The Mavericks’ operating agreement before their current “The Music Lives On” tour to remove such restrictive language. And in Wednesday’s statement, the musicians say Betty is actually being paid handsomely for these shows.

“To clear up any speculation on this topic, we have honored the financial agreement reached with the Malo estate before the tour began, and to date, Betty has received more compensation from the tour than any individual partner in The Mavericks,” wrote the band members on social media. “We’ll continue to honor this agreement, just as our ‘Music Lives On’ Tour has honored the music and legacy of our brother Raul at every turn.”

Betty’s lawyers did not immediately return a request for comment on the band’s statement Wednesday.

Legal disputes over band name rights are not uncommon in the music industry. In the past, such melees have broken out between the members of Stone Temple Pilots, Journey, Jefferson Starship and The Beach Boys. As Billboard previously reported, the question of who truly constitutes the band can be a thorny one, especially when groups change lineups over the years or operate under a web of contracts and LLCs.

As one expert put it to Billboard, “There can be a real disparity between the legal answer, about who owns the trademark, and the emotional answer as to what the name of the band means to the members and to the public.”

#744. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable.

Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did.

Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench.

The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies.

Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II, with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away.

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space, while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase.

That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase.

Super heavy performed its landing burn above the Gulf of Mexico before cutting its engines for a brief moment and exploding in a giant fireball.

This was an intentional detonation, courtesy of the vehicle's flight termination system.

Ship continued on to low Earth orbit, where it deployed a payload of 26 upgraded Starlink Version 3 satellites. It was the second batch of V3 Starlinks delivered during Starship’s recent flight tests, each of which has added what SpaceX says is the equivalent of 10 Falcon 9 Starlink V2 satellite launches worth of data capacity to its orbital constellation.

Flight 15 was also Starship's second-ever mission to orbit, and its longest so far. Ship spent nearly a full day in orbit, circling Earth a total of 14 times. During its jaunt in space, the spacecraft cleared three separate check points, which allowed SpaceX the opportunity to divert the vehicle for an ocean splashdown if needed, and finally was given the green light to attempt the first-ever Ship tower catch.

At approximately 4:18 p.m. EST (2018 GMT, 3:18 p.m. local time in Texas) on Saturday (Nov. 14), the spacecraft broke through the cloud cover that blanketed the skies above Starbase as onlookers watched its bellyflop plunge toward the ground. Moments after becoming visible, Ship ignited its engines for a flip and burn maneuver, which oriented it upright and swung its trajectory into the tightening grip of the chopstick arms of Starbase's "Mechazilla" launch tower.

After a slight sway back and forth suspended above Earth in Mechazilla's embrace, Ship came to a complete rest, hanging motionless as a historic milestone in SpaceX’s pursuit of fully reusable spaceflight.

It hung there overnight as engineers, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, inspected the spacecraft. Ship was lowered on Sunday (Nov. 15) and transported back to SpaceX's Starbase hanger bay for further checkouts.

SpaceX has not yet said whether Ship 42 will fly again, but its return gives engineers a chance to examine how the spacecraft held up through launch, nearly a day in orbit and atmospheric reentry.

Those findings will help inform upcoming flights as SpaceX ramps up production to continue testing Starship's capabilities.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#742. The Hilarious Reason Channing Tatum Is “Useless” to Daughter Everly

Channing Tatum brought his instincts as a dad to his new movie Josephine, in theaters Nov. 20, but as he exclusively told E! News, those instincts don’t extend to his daughter Everly’s dance lessons.

Channing Tatum may not be able to step up as a dance teacher.

Though the Step Up actor may have plenty of dance scenes throughout his filmography, he considers himself more sporty, which isn’t exactly helpful to his and ex-wife Jenna Dewan’s “dancey” 13-year-old daughter Everly.

“All my years of sports are absolutely useless,” Tatum told E! News’ Will Marfuggi in an exclusive interview. “I can help a little dance, but she picked a certain style of dance that I also cannot help with: Irish Celtic dancing. So, I'm useless to her.”

In fact, when the 46-year-old attends Everly’s Irish step dance recitals, he admitted, “I have to look at her instructor when she comes off and I'm like, ‘Was it good? It looked good to me.’”

Still, the She’s The Man actor knows he isn’t completely useless to Everly. As he joked about telling his daughter, “I’m like, ‘If you ever want to throw a football 100 yards, let me know.’”

While Tatum’s ability to recognize his strengths pays off when parenting Everly, it also helped him prepare for his new film Josephine.

In the movie—in select theaters beginning Nov. 20, before expanding nationwide Dec. 4—he and Gemma Chan play a couple who have to console their daughter, played by Mason Reeves, after she witnesses a heinous crime.

“There was a lot of the character that was my instincts,” Tatum explained, before noting he wanted to give his best effort for director Beth de Araújo. “I just wanted to be able to have given her as much to work with inside of that because sometimes pushing really hard is what is what really works.”

Regardless of the effort that the 21 Jump Street star puts into his work, he knows he’ll “never be cool” to Everly, no matter how many of his movies she’s seen.

“She has seen tons of them,” he told E! last year. “She’s like, ‘Whatever, I don’t wanna see those.’ She acts like she doesn’t care.”

Josephine hits select theaters on Nov. 20 and will expand nationwide Dec. 4.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

#739. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

#737. Dakota Johnson Is 50 Shades Sleeker With "Off Black" Hair Makeover

Dakota Johnson darkened her hair to a shade of "off black" thanks to colorist Tracey Cunningham before stepping out for a romantic date night with MGK.

Dakota Johnson just said "laters, baby" to her dirty blonde hair.

Seven months after lightening her signature brunette locks, the Fifty shades of Grey alum went back to her dark roots with what her colorist Tracey Cunningham described as an "off black" hair makeover.

To keep her blackish brown tresses glossy, the hairstylist used products from Schwarzkopf Professional's IGORA VIBRANCE line, according to a press release from the brand.

"@dakotajohnson went lighter for a movie—then came home and shot the cover of Vogue," Cunningham wrote in an Instagram post last month. "And as soon as the Vogue shoot was done, we took her darker again for her next project!"

And Johnson knew just where to show off her new 'do: a date night with Machine Gun Kelly. On Nov. 11, the 37-year-old stepped out in Los Angeles with her raven-colored hair and an oversized tiger-striped coat with a black fur collar.

As she exited a recording studio, MGK—clad in baggy jeans, a white T-shirt and a bright red beanie—proved to be a true gentleman as he took her hand and helped her down the stairs.

But while Johnson is down to switch up her hair color once in a while, she'll never get rid of her iconic fringe.

“I've had bangs since I was a child,” she told Vogue last year. “I cut them myself. I’ve had the same haircut my entire life, apart from between the ages of about 10 and 14. I just feel like myself with bangs.”

However, the Verity star would love to go "without having to trim it all the time."

"I always travel with scissors and love to drink a martini while trimming my own bangs," she quipped, adding that there have been times when she accidentally messed up. "Not every time, but yes."

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.

The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.

"Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites."

Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.

The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.

"For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn."

For comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or New York, according to OwnStarMap. In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.

The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation. Satellite companies plan to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.

Satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.

The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

"This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Reflect Orbital is moving forward with its plan to place mirrors in Earth orbit to produce and sell sunlight after dark.

The goal is to extend the hours and output of solar farms globally, "making clean power dispatchable and available when you need it," the California-based startup explains on its website.

Reflect Orbital has made significant progress to date. On Tuesday (Nov. 10), for example, the company announced it had secured $73.5 million in new funding, boosting its total raise to more than $100 million. It has also gotten a formal go-ahead from the U.S. government to try out the concept in space and is currently readying its first test satellite, which is expected to launch in the second quarter of 2027. The identity of the launch provider is being kept under wraps at this time, the firm told Space.com.

Reflect Orbital recently conducted a ground-based test in California, lighting up a mountainous area to practice search and rescue (SAR) techniques.

On Oct. 10, the space startup set up spotlights near Lone Pine, California to simulate the illumination its proposed satellites could provide — controlled lighting without the need for any ground infrastructure. "This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power," the company explained in an Oct. 14 statement.

The October illumination test ran from 7 p.m. to midnight and involved members of the China Lake Mountain Rescue Group (CLMRG), who practiced with night-time equipment.

CLMRG is an all-volunteer activity, operating under the auspices of the Kern County Sheriff's Office providing SAR services on an on-call basis at no cost.

"Together with local search-and-rescue and disaster response groups, we carried out a fully permitted nighttime demonstration of our responsive lighting service," a Reflect Orbital spokesperson told Space.com in response to an inquiry about the exercise. "Search-and-rescue and disaster response teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who will use our technology."

Mobile lighting gear was mounted on Horseshoe Meadows Road to provide a spot of light similar to the ones that Reflect Orbital satellites are expected to deliver. "The aim was to create a precise, realistic simulation of our service, so emergency responders could see how it will perform in real scenarios," Reflect Orbital said.

The brightness of the spot was roughly 0.7 lumens.

Reflect Orbital added that it will keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever the company operates, to show how its technology can help save lives.

"We're committed to learning incrementally about our technology and its impacts, and from potential customers and stakeholders, ahead of our planned satellite operations," the company stated.

In last month's illumination experiment, Reflect Orbital secured permits in advance, filed a NOTAM (a notice to pilots), notified Edwards Air Force Base and coordinated with the local sheriff's department. Area residents were also notified about the test ahead of time.

In a related development, Reflect Orbital has announced the purchase of two Skyroot Aerospace launches to deploy some of its spacecraft. Skyroot's Vikram-1 launcher is a product of India's private space sector, first flying from the nation's Sriharikota launch site last July. That flight was a landmark success, as Vikram-1 became the first private Indian rocket ever to reach orbit.

"These dedicated launches provide assured schedule and capacity, and complement Reflect Orbital's other planned launches from sites in the United States," Reflect Orbital explained in a different Oct. 14 statement.

Reflect Orbital says its approach is "incremental and test-and-learn." The company has been granted a license from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for one satellite. That mission will test the technology, including built-in safeguards governing precisely how, where and when the sunlight service is delivered.

"It will provide real-world data that shapes the design of future satellites," Reflect Orbital said, "the markets we serve, how we engage communities and the operational practices we put in place. We expect this to be the first of several test missions."

Reflect Orbital wants to be operating at least 50,000 of its mirror satellites in orbit by 2035. Not surprisingly, many people in the astronomy and stargazer communities have a dim view of this plan, saying it will generate light pollution that significantly degrades the night sky.

Reflect Orbital counters that most people and most places will never see this light. Customers will require permits, signoff from local authorities and "Know Your Customer compliance" to receive the service. Every service will require multi-layer approval, the company says, and if people do not want the light, they will not receive it.

Reflect Orbital also claims that it can maintain exclusion zones covering astronomical observation sites.

"Our satellites will be default-off when idle and constellation vehicles are designed to stay under +7 stellar magnitude for all non-serving attitudes. We're able to dim the brightness of the service and turn it off at any stage," the company's website states.

Reflect Orbital also notes that it's an industry member of the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Center for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky.

The company says that it's collaborating with the IAU on an observing campaign for when the service is operational and is also working on a coordination agreement with the U.S. National Science Foundation.

"We've engaged extensively with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other stakeholders," Reflect Orbital stated. "Their feedback has meaningfully informed the design of our spacecraft and operational plans. We continue to welcome scientific exploration of how novel technology could deliver a lot of benefits to the world."

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. #732. Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

Taylor Swift stepped out for her first CMA Awards appearance in 10 years, and her red carpet look for the Nov. 18 ceremony is sure to be remembered evermore.

Taylor swift wore her best dress, fearless to the 2026 Country Music Associate Awards.

After all, it felt like a perfect night to dress up considering the “22” hitmaker attended the Nov. 18 event at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, Tenn., for the first time in 10 years.

And it would be safe and sound to assume that Swift will be performing her 2026 single “I Knew It, I Knew You” from Toy Story 5, which is nominated for Single of the Year at the Lainey Wilson-hosted event.

“Writing this song felt like a musical departure and coming home at the same time,” Swift—who tied the knot with Travis Kelce July 3—said of the track on Instagram June 5. “Creating something for Jessie was a new challenge and also felt like second nature all at once. In addition to the Toy Story team, it was the “Opalite” hitmaker’s longtime collaborator Jack Antonoff who helped her get the track out of the woods.

And going back to her country roots was made even easier with the film’s director Andrew Stanton standing ten toes down for Swift’s involvement in the Disney movie.

#730. Ella Langley Becomes First Act to Earn Top Two of TouchTunes Frontline Chart

"Choosin' Texas" was the most-played song of the third quarter of 2026 on TouchTunes jukeboxes, while Langley's "Be Her" is No. 2 on the Frontline list.

For the first time since the inception of the TouchTunes Frontline and Catalog charts in 2024, the same artist occupies the top two positions of either ranking.

Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” remains at No. 1 on the Frontline Chart for the third quarter of 2026, and Langley’s “Be Her” zooms to No. 2. Related Noah Kahan Reacts to 2027 Grammy Nominations Snub: 'I Was In My Feelings for a Sec' 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Revs Its Engines & Leads 2026 Game Awards Nominations: Full List Cody Johnson on Why He's Skipping 2026 CMA Awards: 'Going 100 MPH All the Time Isn't Healthy' Explore Ella Langley See latest videos, charts and news

The TouchTunes charts for the third quarter of 2026 track the most played songs and artists on TouchTunes jukeboxes from July 1 to Sept. 30, 2026, with the Frontline ranking inclusive of music released in the last 18 months, followed by the Catalog tally for any music that was released more than 18 months ago. The TouchTunes Artists Chart tracks the same period, combining an artist’s plays across both rankings. TouchTunes has jukeboxes in more than 60,000 locations worldwide. Its data is not factored into other Billboard charts.

“Choosin’ Texas” has spent the entirety of 2026 at No. 1 on the Frontline Chart, after debuting at No. 2 for the fourth quarter of 2025. But while the rankings have seen similarly dominant leaders — think Shaboozey’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” and, on Catalog, Chris Stapleton’s “Tennessee Whiskey” — Q3 of 2026 marks the first time one of those acts was able to occupy the entire top two of one of the tallies, with “Be Her” up to No. 2 on Frontline after reaching No. 3 in the second quarter of the year.

In all, Langley is featured on the Frontline survey five times, four as a lead act (her Morgan Wallen duet “I Can’t Love You Anymore” at No. 11 and “Dandelion” at No. 23) and once as the featured performer on BigXthaPlug’s “Hell at Night” at No. 6. She also appears on Catalog at No. 7 via “You Look Like You Love Me,” a duet with Riley Green. Combined, that puts her at No. 2 on the TouchTunes Artists Chart for another quarter, behind perennial No. 1 Wallen.

Following Langley, there’s quite the turnover on Frontline for the latest quarter, with nine debuts among the 25-position chart. Yung Miami’s “Spend Dat” leads the pack at No. 3, followed by Stella Lefty’s “Boston” at No. 4.

“Tennessee Whiskey” remains top dog on Catalog, with Toby Keith’s “I Love This Bar” rising to No. 2. The chart features a top-10 debut in Wallen’s “I’m the Problem,” which bows at No. 8 after graduating to Catalog from Frontline, where it had been No. 2 for Q2.

The August death of Dolly Parton drives a pair of the country legend’s songs onto Catalog in “Jolene” at No. 6 and “9 to 5” at No. 15, while Parton herself bows at No. 7 on the Artists Chart.

Yet again, it’s rock that leads the overall genre ranking for catalog titles, accounting for 37% of plays in the third quarter, down 3% from the second. Country leads frontline-specific songs with 43% of all plays.

#729. Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Amber Dance is a freelance science writer near Los Angeles, California.

A mix of microorganisms from a human faecal sample, imaged using a scanning electron microscope. Credit: Steve Gschmeissner/Science Photo Library

First, the good news: I have 133 microbial species living in my gut. That’s a collection that ranks as ‘excellent’ according to NirvanaBiome, the company in Germantown, Maryland, that analysed my stool sample. The firm based its rating on the overall diversity of my gut’s residents plus my levels of specific beneficial and undesirable species.

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease

But then came a second, less promising assessment: Viome in Bellevue, Washington, identified only 61 kinds of active microorganism in my gut and suggested that some of them were not performing optimally. Viome recommended dietary changes and offered customized supplements to improve my health.

I was intrigued by the results, but also flummoxed by the different messages. That’s not an uncommon response, says microbiologist Rob Knight, director of the Center for Microbiome Innovation at the University of California, San Diego. When scientists tested a handful of microbiome testing kits alongside one another in formal studies, they found wide discrepancies in the results. These differences make it hard to understand or really trust the findings from any given provider, says Diane Hoffmann, director of the Law and Health Care programme at the University of Maryland in Baltimore, who co-authored one of those studies.

The companies stand by their products. “Of course there’s variability,” says Kelly Moffat, chief operations officer for Cmbio in Germantown, which does the laboratory work and genetic sequencing for NirvanaBiome. “There has to be because this is complex testing.”

Momo Vuyisich, chief science officer at Viome’s lab in Bothwell, Washington, also says he was unsurprised by the degree of variation found by formal studies. Labs use different methods to extract, sequence and analyse microbial genetic material. Viome, for example, sequences RNA rather than DNA, allowing it to uncover microbial gene activity, rather than only the presence of genes. Vuyisich argues that this is more relevant to human health. And he says that although every method will have biases, as long as a consumer sticks with the same provider, it should produce results that are comparable over time.

Interest in these kinds of test is booming. “There’s so much public enthusiasm and excitement about the microbiome,” says Knight. Some customers are simply curious about the microscopic beings that live inside them and potentially affect their health; others have health conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and hope that their gut microbes will reveal the underlying cause or a path to better health.

Although people can order the tests and follow their recommendations without the help of a medical professional, some people are bringing the findings to their physicians. “I groan when I see someone come in with a microbiome test,” says Fergus Shanahan, a gastroenterologist and immunologist at University College Cork in Ireland, who has spent much of his career studying the microbiome. For someone struggling with gut health, a consumer microbiome profile isn’t usually specific enough to help. And if there’s a concern about an infection, such as Clostridioides difficile, it’s more straightforward to test for known pathogens than to assess the entire microbial community.

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain

Microbiologists and gasteroenterologists who spoke to Nature generally agreed that microbiome testing has the potential to both reflect and promote health, but many said that the science isn’t yet mature enough to support microbiome testing for most consumers. In their view, the limited clinical usefulness of today’s consumer tests can make them poor value for money (costing around US$100–300). The specialists warn that acting on advice that doesn’t come from clinicians could lead customers to adopt unnecessarily restrictive diets or delay appropriate medical assessment. Critics say that consumer microbiome testing needs more regulatory scrutiny and oversight.

“This is an industry that’s running wild,” says genomicist Jacques Ravel, director of the Center for Advanced Microbiome Research and Innovation at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in Baltimore and a co-author on one of the studies that tested several providers. With regards to testing methods, he says, “there’s no standard”.

Moffat says, “I think the jury’s out on exactly what it is that we can actionably do today based on this data.” But she says that microbiome profiles, combined with other testing such as gut metabolomics, could yield interesting and useful health information.

The gut microbiome has emerged as an incredible correlate of overall health. From immune-system function to metabolism, skin disorders and mental health, study after study has found links between a person’s well-being and the trillions of microbes that live in their digestive tract. The premise of a head count of these species and assessment of their actions, to monitor and improve gut health in a personalized way, certainly sounds appealing. Viome’s website, for example, promises: “No more trial and error … Follow a plan built precisely for you.”

Companies can identify species and, on the basis of those lists, infer what the microbes are probably doing, such as manufacturing metabolites or inciting inflammation. But running even the simplest microbiome testing is expensive, says Alessandra Cervino, research director at PiLeJe, a science-based food-supplement company in Paris. She says her microbiome testing company, Luxia Scientific, closed in 2024 for financial reasons.

Some microbiome testing firms recommend fermented foods, such as kombucha, for gut health.Credit: Deb Lindsey for The Washington Post via Getty

Many testing companies also offer lifestyle and nutritional advice or sell supplements. For example, Viome analysed diverse functions performed by the microbes in my gut, such as digestive efficiency, gas production and serotonin manufacture. I then received a detailed eating plan — which told me to eschew broccoli and load up on pecans, among other suggestions — along with an offer for precision supplements and probiotics with a price tag of more than $150 a month. Although it’s hard to change the composition of microbes in one’s gut, alterations in diet or even simply ageing can shift their activities, says Vuyisich. The company recommends re-testing every four to six months to check for shifts and update the plan.

He points to 19 peer-reviewed publications by Viome as evidence of the company’s rigour (see go.nature.com/4actdhq). For example, the firm’s analysis for consumers is supported, in part, by published data on how gut microbes influence individuals’ responses to glucose in various foods, based on 550 people in the United States who collectively ate more than 30,000 meals while wearing glucose monitors1. The company validated those findings in a further cohort in Japan, Vuyisich says, but those data are not published.

Microbiome tests are not created equal, says Tim Spector, a physician-scientist at King’s College London and co-founder of London-based ZOE, which offers microbiome testing and a supplement in addition to a gut-health app that I’ve been playing with. ZOE’s products, Spector says, are backed by research on thousands of people. “There definitely are some not-so-good players out there that give this field a bad name,” he says. “It’s not easy to do this well.”

There are also several ways to do microbe testing; companies take varying approaches that yield disparate results, as at least two studies have shown. Scientists at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Gaithersburg, Maryland, shipped homogenized stool samples from one person to seven companies2. NIST’s remit is researching and applying standards for measurement. This experiment was a step towards understanding the diversity of testing options out there, says one of the study authors, NIST microbiologist Stephanie Servetas, who is based in Sheridan, Wyoming. The researchers didn’t name the companies in their report because they wanted to focus attention on the comparison between tests rather than perceived accuracy of any individual provider.

The result: “Companies produce strikingly different results,” says co-author Scott Jackson, a molecular geneticist who used to direct the NIST microbiology program and is now a consultant in Saint Michaels, Maryland. “They couldn’t even agree on what’s healthy and unhealthy,” Jackson says. The microbe lists ranged from 34 to 906 identified genera; only 3 of which showed up in all reports. In fact, the results were as varied from company to company as they would be for different people, despite all tests being done on samples from the same individual.

A European and Canadian team obtained similar outcomes when they sent homogenized samples from one person’s stool to six companies, also anonymized. Three companies rated the microbial diversity as “excellent” or “good”; two called it “average”; one said it was “unfavourable”3. The results were so variable, that at least some of them must be lacking in validation or standardization, says co-author Céline Druart, executive director of the Pharmabiotic Research Institute (PRI) in Brussels, a non-profit organization specializing in regulation of microbiome innovations. “It’s very difficult to make a conclusion,” she says.

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments

This broad divergence in results is not surprising, says Jack Gilbert, director of the Microbiome and Metagenomics Center at the University of California, San Diego. The variation starts at sampling: scoop a bit of faecal matter into a tube, stab it with a coring device or swipe the sampler across some used toilet paper; ship it off as-is, or in some kind of preservative (as both Viome’s and NirvanaBiome’s kits asked me to). Each option could influence the balance of the microbes that are collected and what survives to be sequenced.

In the lab, Servetas says the method by which the researchers extract genetic material from a sample is a big source of divergence. Gentler protocols will bias a sample towards microbes that are easy to crack open, whereas harsher methods will capture a higher share of species with tougher exteriors.

After sequencing, another major source of difference, says Knight, is the bioinformatics pipeline that labs use. What length or number of genetic sequences is required to consider a microbe present? What list of sequences and microbes are they using as a reference? “All bets are off when you then computationally analyse it with your favourite method,” says Knight.

Would companies support having standards to validate their tests? “We are really big advocates on really having a standard here,” says Kimberley Sukhum, chief science officer at Tiny Health in Austin, Texas, which offers gut microbiome tests as well as vaginal microbiome tests.

But it’s hard to set those standards, in part because there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample. Compare that with, say, a blood-glucose test; a lab can get a known value from a standard sample either right or wrong. But the microbiome, in its glorious complexity, does not allow for such simple validation. NIST has used mixed human donor samples to develop a standard4. And Tiny Health has experimented with generating a reference for benchmarking from synthetic communities. It was built from individual microbial species rather than sampled from faeces5. But neither of those standards is exactly like the microbiome of an individual person.

Even if labs could assess a microbiome perfectly, they’d still have a problem: there’s no defined healthy microbiome like there is one range of healthy blood-glucose levels. Each person’s microbiome is unique, like a fingerprint. There are infinitely many ways to have a healthy microbiome, and infinitely many ways to have an unhealthy one, says Shanahan; it’s not entirely clear how to draw a line between the two.

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders

Companies must compare customer microbiomes with some standard of health, but these vary too. They might be based on past customers or large, public databases. But microbiomes differ considerably depending on factors such as ethnicity, sex, age, recent antibiotic use or even whether someone was born by caesarean section.

#728. 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966

It was a spectacle many regard as the greatest meteor display on record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky.

At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history.

It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

"I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights.

"I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound.

"I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust.

"I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever."

"I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time.

"The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch.

"We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise.

"As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event."

"I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!"

"I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep."

"Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away"

"I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory.

"My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son.

"He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies.

"I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs.

"That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning.

"I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father.

"That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting."

Not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason.

Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas.

"Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.'

"Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars."

Rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to New York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display.

But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight.

"After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'"

The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars.

Most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm.

The Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. And 1966 wasn't the last time the Leonids put on an extraordinary show. In 1999, 2001 and 2002, the Leonids once again reached meteor-storm levels, producing thousands of meteors per hour at their peaks. The shows aren't over yet! With comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle due to return in 2031, astronomers are already looking ahead to what the following years could bring.

A study released in August 2026 predicts potentially impressive Leonid displays in 2033 and 2034, with peak rates exceeding 1,000 meteors per hour. However, these forecasts remain uncertain, and a repeat of the extraordinary 1966 storm is far from guaranteed.

For now, we'll just have to wait and see.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.
