#727. Wael Mohya could make German football history at 17

At just 17, Gladbach forward Wael Mohya has earned his first Germany call-up. The dual-national talent has chosen the DFB path for now — and could soon make modern national-team history.

If you watch the Bundesliga, then you'll know Wael Mohya is a fast-footed, quick-thinking footballer. But not even the 17-year-old (Mohya turns 18 on December 31) Borussia Mönchengladbach youngster would have expected to be called up to the Germany squad so soon.

"Of course, I was absolutely thrilled. It means a great, great deal to me. I think everyone dreams of being selected for the national team at some point," Mohya said.

"And the fact that it's come to this now is, of course, just awesome and makes me very proud."

Mohya was at the gym when the call came in. He then shared the good news with his parents over dinner. "They started crying," the teenager said in a video posted on Gladbach's social media channels.

The youngster, who was born in a small town east of Düsseldorf, smiles and laughs a lot in interviews. He is always friendly, and in a good mood. On the field, too, he exudes the lightheartedness and carefree spirit of a 17-year-old.

As a technically skilled and creative player, Mohya often seeks out one-on-one situations and puts his opponents under pressure with quick dribbles. In nine Bundesliga appearances this season, Mohya has scored twice and delivered one assist.

"He's so cool and just plays really well. It's fun to watch him," Borussia coach Alexander Blessin said recently.

"Wael brings a lot to the team with his laid-back attitude on the field. He's not afraid to take risks, no matter how much pressure there is," added Gladbach's sporting director Rouven Schröder at a talk show on Sport1.

Borussia Mönchengladbach has been Mohya's sporting home since he was seven years old. Last season, previous head coach Eugen Polanski promoted him to the first team, and in December 2025, Mohya made his Bundesliga debut. Against Wolfsburg, aged 16 years and 347 days old, he became the youngest Bundesliga player in the club's history.

Mohya also recently completed a voluntary social year at an elementary school in Mönchengladbach. This is a program in Germany for young people who volunteer in the social sector — at hospitals, schools, or nursing homes, for example — for about six to 18 months. They gain work experience, help others, and earn a little money.

At the school's open all-day care program, Mohya helped serve meals, assisted children with their homework, and played with them. That's also where his nickname comes from. Because a girl hadn't understood his first name correctly or couldn't pronounce it, she called him "Waffel." Now, that name has stuck.

Even before being called up to the Germany team, clubs in the Bundesliga and across Europe's top leagues had taken notice of Mohya and were trying to sign him. His contract with Borussia Mönchengladbach runs through 2028.

With Gladbach currently in a relegation battle, his future appears likely to be elsewhere. If the club wants to generate transfer revenue from its biggest talent, next summer would likely be the opportunity to sell him — unless he extends his contract with Borussia.

The 17-year-old's career is managed by his parents. Whichever club can convince them that their son is in good hands and help him reach his full potential likely has the best chance of securing Mohya's signing.

Mohya himself says he doesn't even know how much he's currently earning at Gladbach.

"My parents take care of all that," he told Bild recently. "I get a monthly allowance, which is more than enough for me."

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp recently revealed how much he had enjoyed his conversations with the youngster.

"The conversations I had with him were great," Klopp said with a laugh. "I wasn't that confident at 17, but then again, I wasn't that good either."

Since Mohya's parents are from Morocco, their son also holds Moroccan citizenship. As a result, he could have played for Morocco, but he has now decided against it. In fact, the Moroccan football association had been actively courting Mohya as early as last year and had already reached out to him in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup.

Now, like Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib, Mohya will continue to play in the German jersey, unlike Schalke's Soufiane El-Faouzi, who chose Morocco, or Bayer Leverkusen's Ibrahim Maza, who likely would have been selected by Klopp as well if he hadn't already opted for Algeria.

For Mohya, who played for Germany's youth teams from the U16s through to the U21s, the door to Morocco remains open, even if he does play for Germany. According to FIFA regulations, players under the age of 21 can change national teams before their fourth international match (whether a competitive or friendly match), provided that none of those matches take place during a World Cup or a continental tournament such as the European Championship, Copa America, or Africa Cup of Nations.

If Mohya plays in the upcoming UEFA Nations League games in Serbia or against the Netherlands, another record is on the horizon. Although there were two even younger players who made their debuts in the Germany jersey — Willy Baumgärtner in 1908 (at 17 years and 104 days) and Marius Hiller in 1910 (at 17 years and 241 days) — the era in which they debuted is hardly comparable. And so, while Wael Mohya would rank third overall on the list, he would become the youngest Germany player in the modern era. The youngest to date was Hamburg legend Uwe Seeler in 1954, aged 17 years and 345 days.

#726. Underscores Is First Transgender Woman Nominated for Best Dance/Electronic Recording Grammy

The 2027 nominations in this category are also significant for the number of women nominated.

The Grammys are making history this year, with first-time nominee Underscores now the first out transgender woman to be nominated for best dance/electronic recording. The artist got the nod for “Music,” from her March album U.

Many transgender women have paved the way for this accomplishment, with SOPHIE, Kim Petras, Arca, Honey Dijon, Wendy Carlos, Jackie Shane and Teddy Geiger all receiving nominations over the years. In 2023, Petras became the first transgender woman to win a Grammy, when she got the award for best pop duo/group performance for her Sam Smith collab “Unholy.”

In her acceptance speech, Petras acknowledged this achievement, saying, “I just want to thank all the incredible transgender legends before me who kicked these doors open for me so I could be here tonight. SOPHIE especially, my friend who passed away two years ago who told me this would happen and always believed in me… Madonna for fighting for LGBTQ rights. I don’t think I could be here without Madonna. My mother — I grew up next to a highway in nowhere Germany and my mother believed me that I was a girl, and I wouldn’t be here without her and her support.”

Trans women are also making history elsewhere at the 2027 Grammys, with Geese’s Emily Green being the first out trans woman nominated for best new artist, best rock performance, best alternative music performance, best alternative music album and best rock song.

The 2027 dance/electronic recording category is also significant for the number of woman nominated, with Madonna’s “I Feel So Free,” Slayyyter’s “Crank” and Tinashe’s “Melatonin” all nominated alongside Underscores and fellow nominees Fred again.. (for “Lights Burn Dimmer”) and Tame Impala (for “My Old Ways”).

This marks the first time four solo women acts were nominated for best dance/electronic recording since 2000, when the nominees were Gloria Estefan for “Don’t Let This Moment End,” Jennifer Lopez for “Waiting For Tonight,” Donna Summer for “I Will Go With You (Con te Partirò),” Fatboy Slim for “Praise You” and Cher for “Believe,” with this latter song winning the award.

Astronauts get tasked with all kinds of weird science aboard the International Space Station. Recently, NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins got to work supporting an ongoing experiment that includes 3D-printing human cells and tissues in space.

Aboard the space station, astronauts have a multitude of responsibilities ranging from station maintenance and repairs on spacewalks to daily exercise and a wide variety of scientific research.

Watkins recently shared a snapshot captured by her crewmate Anil Menon that showcases her experience working on an experiment called InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing that takes place inside the station's Life Sciences Glovebox, a contained research space and one of Watkins favorite places to work on the space station, she shared on social media.

In the image she is gloved-up with both her hands and arms covered in the sealed glovebox while she mixes samples of living cells with a bioink, a mixture she then inserts into a specialized cartridge, NASA shared.

This experiment that Watkins is working on "leverages the microgravity environment of ISS to 3D print cells and manufacture human liver, kidney, and cartilage tissue. Just one of many examples of how we’re using this amazing orbital national laboratory to reshape our understanding of biology, medicine, and engineering, and improve life on Earth!" Watkins shared online.

This experiment is designed to explore 3D printing human cartilage tissue in microgravity. The experiment aims to one day support future human patients both in space and on Earth.

When you think of the research that happens in space, 3D-printing human cells might not be the first thing to come to mind. But because of the unique microgravity environment onboard the ISS, it is the perfect home for even the strangest of biological experiments.

On the space station, there is still gravity but objects (and people) remain in a sort of constant freefall, leading to total weightlessness that mimics the complete absence of gravity. This weightlessness allows researchers to test, experiment and explore beyond the gravitational confines of Earth.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. Voyager 1 has gone farther than any other object built by humanity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft.

The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth. And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).

NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.

To celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code: NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence.

The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said.

NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making.

The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1. At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes.

Launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2, is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.)

The public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission. On Thursday (Nov. 19) at 12 p.m. EST (1700 GMT), NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with Voyager mission team members and NASA leadership.

The discussion will cover the current status of both Voyager spacecraft, the unique scientific observations they continue to collect in interstellar space and the engineering challenges involved in keeping the nearly 50-year-old probes operational. A question-and-answer session with members of the media and audience will follow. NASA will also offer a preview of an upcoming Voyager documentary planned for release in 2027, coinciding with the mission's 50th anniversary.

For a mission that has carried humanity's message into interstellar space for nearly half a century, the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day” offers a chance for people back on Earth to mark just how far these pioneering spacecraft have traveled. More details about NASA's automated VGR flasher and step-by-step Morse code instructions are available online.

Samantha Mathewson joined Space.com as an intern in the summer of 2016. She received a B.A. in Journalism and Environmental Science at the University of New Haven, in Connecticut. Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos! You can follow her on Twitter @Sam_Ashley13.

#722. Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms are needed.

For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.

In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.

The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.

Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.

However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.

The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism.

The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW.

Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said.

According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts."

But critics see this as a major weakness.

"The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.

Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

"The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, said the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough."

Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he said, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.

Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.

The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.

For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she said.

As of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

But Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles."

The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive."

The new rules have been in effect for only 10 months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Steinert said fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.

Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.

Such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert said.  However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.

The bank said that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns."

"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.

Sausmikat said Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

Hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards."

This article was originally written in German.

#721. Michael Jackson’s ‘Second Family’ Sues Estate’s Lawyer Over ‘Hush Money’ Sex Abuse Deal

The Cascio siblings, who claim Jackson molested them as children, are accusing celebrity attorney Bryan Freedman of a "despicable betrayal."

A group of siblings who allege they were sexually abused by Michael Jackson as children are suing celebrity lawyer Bryan Freedman over a “despicable betrayal.”

Freedman faces legal malpractice and fraud claims in a Wednesday (Nov. 18) lawsuit, submitted to Los Angeles court and reviewed by Billboard. It’s brought by the five Cascio siblings — Frank, Edward, Dominic, Aldo and Marie-Nicole — as well as Marie-Nicole’s husband, James Porte.

The Cascios grew up with Jackson and once referred to themselves as his “second family.” For years, they staunchly defended the King of Pop against pedophilia claims. But in 2019, they said the HBO documentary Leaving Neverland had deprogrammed them from Jackson’s “brainwashing,” and that they privately began alleging that the star had molested and raped Edward, Dominic, Aldo and Marie-Nicole as children.

Wednesday’s lawsuit alleges that upon these revelations, the Jackson estate enlisted Freedman — a major Hollywood litigator who has represented celebrities like Rebel Wilson, Vin Diesel and Justin Baldoni — “to deceive Plaintiffs into signing a hush-money agreement.” This settlement promised nearly $3.5 million to each of the five Cascio siblings, as long as they never went public with their claims and released all future legal claims over the alleged abuse.

According to the lawsuit, Freedman presented this deal to the family as a “life rights agreement” and did not explain its far-reaching ramifications. The siblings say Freedman dissuaded them from hiring an independent lawyer and said he was their advocate, when in reality he was working on behalf of the estate’s interests.

“He exploited the family’s vulnerability and trust to induce them into signing an unconscionable agreement, which stripped them of valuable legal rights, imposed sweeping confidentiality provisions and shielded Jackson’s estate and representatives from liability,” reads the lawsuit against Freedman.

This agreement has indeed proved inconvenient for the Cascios. They tried earlier this year to sue the Jackson estate for sex trafficking, but a judge ruled that the claims must be handled in confidential arbitration under the clear terms of the 2019 settlement.

Now, the siblings want financial damages from Freedman for putting them in this position. Wednesday’s lawsuit alleges that with a truly independent lawyer, they would have retained their legal rights, or at the very least “negotiated an agreement with a much higher settlement payment that would have been commensurate with Jackson’s molestation of the Cascio family.”

Freedman did not immediately return a request for comment on Wednesday. Reps for the Jackson estate, which is not named as a defendant in this lawsuit, also did not return an inquiry.

The estate has previously characterized the Cascios’ claims as a “desperate money grab,” pointing out that they “spent decades defending and affirming Michael’s innocence” before changing their story. The siblings stated during a 2010 appearance on The Oprah Winfrey Show, for example, that Jackson was “never” inappropriate with them, and Frank wrote in a 2011 memoir, “Michael’s love for children was innocent, and it was profoundly misunderstood.”

Jackson, who died in 2009, was never convicted or held legally liable for any accusation of child sex abuse during his lifetime; he settled a civil claim in 1994 without admitting any wrongdoing, and he was acquitted at a criminal trial in 2005. But such allegations have continued to dog his legacy, most notably when Leaving Neverland amplified claims from two men, Wade Robson and James Safechuck, in disturbing detail.

The Jackson estate vehemently denies all claims of sexual misconduct. It called Leaving Neverland a “one-sided hit job” and sued HBO, successfully getting the documentary removed from streaming. Robson and Safechuck are continuing to litigate civil abuse claims against the estate.

#720. Kylie Cantrall Surprises Fans With Private Acoustic Set in Downtown L.A.

The actress-singer, who broke out with her role as Red in Disney's 'Descendants' movies, took over Moxy Downtown Los Angeles to perform for fans on Tuesday night.

On the heels of her Valley Girl Problems Tour, Kylie Cantrall played a surprise intimate acoustic set in downtown Los Angeles on Tuesday night for a crowd of enthusiastic fans who sang along with all of her tunes.

Cantrall took over Moxy Downtown Los Angeles for the special event, which also celebrated her EP, Valley Girl Problems, which debuted in July. The event was part of Moxy Hotels’ ongoing music series, which brings emerging and buzzy artists together with fans for intimate experiences at Moxy properties around the world (other recent events have featured Ayra Starr in the U.K.). Related Stories Music Mumford & Sons' Ben Lovett to Open New Venue At Brooklyn's Domino Sugar Refinery Lifestyle Kel Mitchell Bringing 'Kel's Burger Fest' to Los Angeles: "It's a Full-On Burger Bonanza"

The actor-singer — who has starred in two of Disney’s Descendants movies, playing Red, daughter of the Queen of Hearts — noted onstage that Los Angeles was her hometown and she was “feeling the love” at Moxy DTLA that night.

After asking how many people were also at her recent tour — many in the audience were — she shared: “That show was a mix of emotions. I was so sad,” she said, and then a fan said she had cried during the show. “I made you cry? That should be a disclaimer on my website: If you’re coming to a Kylie show, there’s a chance you’re going to cry. But you’re going to shake a little ass too,” she quipped. “It’s a mix of both. That’s me in a nutshell honestly — crying and shaking ass at the same time.”

Cantrall said she was missing being on tour when Moxy Hotels reached out about the surprise pop-up L.A. show, and she said jumped at the chance to perform in the intimate venue. Addressing the fans, she continued, “Thank you guys for coming at the last minute.”

She performed four songs at the event, kicking off with “Carrie Bradshaw,” a tribute to Cantrall’s “favorite TV character,” the one played by Sarah Jessica Parker in Sex and the City. “She’s is a fashion icon; she’s kind of a mess as well, but we love her for it,” Cantrall said. (The bar at Moxy DTLA was serving special cocktails in honor of the event that included the Carrie Cosmo and the Valley Girl Martini.)

Next up was “Oversized,” from her previous EP, B.O.Y. (Deluxe). She revealed that she’s a “hoodie stealer,” joking that she had about five of her best friend’s hoodies at her house. In co-writing the song, “I was kind of inspired by this era I was in, dating and dealing with guys with hoodies. … I definitely still have two of (my ex’s) hoodies that I never gave back, but he never asked for them back. And they look better on me anyway,” she joked.

“You know we’re gonna get in our feels for a minute,” she said, introducing the next song, the emotional “Space Between” from Valley Girl Problems. “Now that I’ve been home, I’ve been writing the next album … but I haven’t written any ballads on it so far. That just goes to show you we’re healed. We’re healing slowly day by day. This song is very special to me. If you’re going through something right now, or maybe you’re healing through a situation, maybe even this song helped you heal a little bit.” After, a fan told her that song always makes her cry, to which Cantrall responded that it makes her emotional as well. She also gave the crowd a note of encouragement: “You are so entitled to feeling whatever you’re feeling … and I think the best thing we can do as humans is just try to embrace our imperfections and let that shit go, whether it’s writing it down, talking to someone, therapy, writing music, creating art. … You are never alone.” (Here she quipped that it was her first 18-and-older show, so she didn’t have to censor herself as when she was on tour.)

Cantrall closed the show with “Elastic,” which she said was so frequently requested during her tour that she wound up adding it to her setlist. She wrapped with an a capella sing-along to a few verses of “Valley Girl Problems” to the delight of those inside Moxy DTLA.

Indeed, many of those in attendance sang along with her songs throughout the performance, and Cantrall engaged in some fun banter with the fans. Afterward, she asked the crowd to take a group photo before graciously signing autographs and taking selfies with fans’ phones.

Cantrall recently hit 15 cities across North America as part of her first-ever headlining tour, which kicked off Sept. 25 in Minneapolis and wrapped up Oct. 22 in Los Angeles, her hometown. Next, she’s set to appear on three dates of the Jingle Ball tour (Dec. 1 in Dallas, Dec. 14 in Washington, D.C. and Dec. 15 in Philadelphia). In summer 2025, she toured North America as part of Disney’s Descendants/Zombies: Worlds Collide Tour.

Valley Girl Problems, released via Republic Records, follows on the heels of her debut EP, B.O.Y. The new nine-track EP was produced by Grammy-winning hitmaker Tricky Stewart (Rihanna, Tyla) and written alongside acclaimed songwriter Tayla Parx.

Moxy Hotels says that its music series aims to create a space where Gen Z can be connected with artists, events and moments shaping culture.

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. The lives of NASA's Apollo astronauts depended on it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.

Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff.

First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.

NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.

The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.

But a lunar liftoff? That was something new.

"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.

The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.

But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.

"This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation."

Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.

Lower bleph? Filler? Face lipo? Buccal fat remover? Chin surgery? Nose surgery?!” Pugh continued, slamming the accusations.

The actress said she is “disturbed” by “having my body dissected and pointed at again,” and that she has “spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow” while also experiencing fat shaming “from the moment I started and I have loved everytime I get to tell someone to fuck off when they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I’m not changing that now just because you’ve all said so.”

In a recent Instagram video shared by Evie magazine, a woman analyzed Pugh’s face, placing a side-by-side image of her a few years past beside her recent appearance at the 2026 Governors Awards, saying, “People are saying Florence Pugh has fallen victim to Hollywood’s war on round faces. Don’t get me wrong, Florence Pugh still looks beautiful, but I think we can all collectively agree that Hollywood seems to have this thing against softer features.”

The woman referenced Pugh’s “sculpted, snatched look,” and said that the actress used to have “full, beautiful cheeks,” but now that her “jaw is more defined, her chin is more pointier, her jaws more are sharp, it makes sense why people are wondering if she’s had any work done.” The actress herself commented on Evie’s Instagram post, writing, “Guys. I turned 30. I’m a woman. Body’s and faces change. It’s not that deep. The fact that people can’t even tell between what’s aging and what’s surgery is disturbing. Sadly puppy fluff doesn’t last forever.”

The Oscar nominee denied having surgery or taking the weight-loss drug in her Instagram post. “I have never been on ozempic. I have NEVER done any face surgery. And don’t EVER say that I didn’t make my own nose, I’ve always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!” Pugh shared a photo of herself as a child on her Instagram Story, writing, “I’ve had that baby since day one. No surgery please and thank you very much.”

She further explained that after turning 30, her New Year’s resolution was “to change my relationship with alcohol, and to be able to do at least one pull up in the gym.” The actress also said it’s been “funny to see you all use reference images from times where I was really mentally unhappy and abusing my body and put it next to the image from the governors awards the other night where I am happy and truly respecting my body.”

The Thunderbolts star said that “for the first time in my ENTIRE career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily. I’ve WANTED to move my body and not take it for granted. Guess how much weight I’ve lost in all of that? 2 pounds.”

She also explained that she’s been prioritizing growing muscle because “I think it’s the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do 6 pull ups and lift 110kg. Which I’m sure to many of you isn’t a lot.. but to me?! It’s everything.” On her Instagram Story, Pugh also posted a few videos of her training in the gym.

“I’ve fucking worked so hard to clean my head and clean my body because I don’t want to allow space for negativity in my mind to grow. I’m looking after myself, and that’s literally it,” Pugh wrote, urging her followers to “be mindful” as she’s also previously received negative comments in the past.

“I also want to point out that over the years I have been in the public eye, I have received comments or messages daily about how I look like a pig, that I’m fat and should go on a run, that I shouldn’t be proud of my body, that I SHOULD go on ozempic, that I shouldn’t show my midriff because I shouldn’t be proud of it. (The size of my thighs even made it into a movie review after I played Saraya the WWE wrestler which will never not be mind blowing),” Pugh added.

“I’ve always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that. But now this..? I’m asking us all to just be mindful. We are all real people, living real lives,” she concluded.

"Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update.

The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.

The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)

That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.)

NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #716. Democracy study: One-quarter of Germans want a right-wing authoritarian dictatorship

The far-right AfD's electoral successes point to a new trend in Germany: Prejudice, resentment, and extremism are on the rise. A new study suggests satisfaction with democracy is at a low ebb.

Satisfaction with democracy in Germany has hit a new low, while the past is being idealized, and people are expressing a longing for a radical break. Antisemitic sentiments and the desire for an authoritarian leader are also on the rise. These are key findings of the authoritarianism study presented Wednesday in Berlin, which has been conducted every two years since 2002.

The study, led by the Else Frenkel-Brunswik Institute for Democracy Research at the University of Leipzig, is based on the answers to a questionnaire by 2,507 respondents, who the researchers say are a representative cross-section of the German population.

For the first time since the study series began, approval of democracy as an idea fell just below the 90% mark, which the study said is primarily attributable to a loss of trust among respondents in the former East Germany (85.7%). The decline in approval of democracy as experienced in everyday life is even more severe: Nationwide, only one-third are satisfied with democracy, with figures having fallen sharply both in eastern (22.8%) and western (36%) states.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The growing rejection of democracy is also reflected in the desire for some kind of authoritarian nationalist government: Just under a quarter of respondents explicitly supported the idea of a "single strong party that embodies the national community as a whole." In the east, the figure stands at 30.9%, above the Germany-wide average of 22.3%.

"Our democracy is under great pressure. It has lost acceptance among the general population. It is alarming how much an authoritarian yearning is taking its place," concluded social psychologist and study author Oliver Decker.

Far-right attitudes have risen for the second consecutive year. Of particular note in the study was what the researchers called a chauvinistic national pride, which, with 19.9% approval, has reached its highest level since the study series began. The proportion of people with a consistently far-right worldview has reached 6.9%, the highest level since 2014, the study found.

Just under 15% of respondents said they explicitly believe that "everything has to fall apart so that something new can emerge," while nearly one in three respondents believes that "something radical is needed for the current state of affairs to change." Another 29.1% agree with this to some extent.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to the study, those who share this yearning for catastrophe exhibit significantly stronger antisemitic sentiments — and both are linked to a preference for certain political parties. The study found that a large proportion of eligible voters with this orientation favor the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Through its violent rhetoric, the AfD promises to realize the political goals of far-right ideology," the study said. The party's form and content, in other words, correspond exactly to the message that a significant portion of the population wants to hear. "It offers a political home to those who adhere to far-right thinking, while at the same time presenting itself as capable of connecting with a broad segment of society."

Study co-author Johannes Kiess calls on political leaders at all levels to find countermeasures. "The rejection of the present state of the world must be countered with compelling democratic alternatives and the ability to take political action today," he said. This also applies to the significant rise in antisemitism, which has more than doubled since 2022.

When asked about the motives behind antisemitic attitudes, the results show that for 16% of respondents, the policies of Israel's government are the decisive factor. This, too, is a record high in the context of the long-term study. While the figure in 2020 was significantly higher in the east (12%) than in the west (8.4%), the figures have since converged. Antisemitism related to Israel is actually slightly stronger in western than in eastern states.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hostility toward Muslims is also on the rise. It peaked at over 40% in 2018, before dropping to well below 30%, and currently stands at 34.1%. These figures are based on two statements respondents were asked to agree with in each survey: "Muslims should be prohibited from immigrating to Germany" and "because of the many Muslims here, I sometimes feel like a stranger in my own country."

Misogyny is another issue regularly surveyed in the study. In the current survey, 18.3% agreed with anti-feminist statements. Notably, until now, a higher proportion of East Germans had been opposed to feminist causes. As recently as 2024, the difference between the former East (34.6%) and West (19.6%) was enormous. Two years later, the figure in the east has halved to 17.8%, while in western Germany it has fallen only slightly to 18.4%.

Despite the negative trend, there is a glimmer of hope at the end of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study: While the results are "alarming," long-term trends show that a reversal of this trend is possible: "In earlier surveys, far-right statements already achieved high approval ratings, which then declined again in subsequent years. In addition to the influence of societal crises, political action and its societal perception are of central importance."

This article was originally written in German. It was first published on November 11 and later edited for clarity.

#715. How to make AI data centres more sustainable

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

AI companies must engage with those who oppose the expansion of data centres.Credit: Michael M. Santiago/Getty

Around the world, people are demanding a halt to the proliferation of data centres — racks of computers, housed in warehouses, that are powering the boom in artificial intelligence. Communities worry that existing infrastructure will not be able to handle the surge in demand for electricity and water, and that data centres’ energy demands will cause environmental and health problems, including increases in air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. The question of whether AI is going to stall climate action is explored in the first of a three-part Nature Podcast (Nature https://doi.org/rzqs; 2026).

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

People have many concerns about the way AI is being developed, including how it might affect safety, security and jobs. Where energy is concerned, however, any added demand for computing power can, and must, be met in smart, sustainable ways, not by burning more fossil fuels. Achieving this will take some creative thinking, and researchers need to be closely involved. Many argue that there are alternatives to relying on energy-intensive data centres, such as AI models that can run on individual computers or institutional servers, thereby consuming much less power than those run using cloud services. Efforts to develop such options need to be better funded.

Future projections of data centres’ energy demands are hard to make, because they are based on assumptions that could change. If current global trends continue, electricity consumption by data centres will go on rising. Between 2017 and 2024, it grew by around 12% per year. Figures for 2024 from the International Energy Agency (IEA), based in Paris, show most of this demand coming from three regions: the United States (45%), China (25%) and Europe (15%).

The Electric Power Research Institute, a non-profit organization in Palo Alto, California, has projected that the continued growth of US data centres could add up to 94 gigawatts of demand by 2030, equivalent to 17% of the country’s electricity consumption. Data centres currently consume more than 1.5% of the world’s electricity supply, and the IEA’s projections indicate that this figure will more than double in the next few years. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than Japan, the agency says.

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

There are serious concerns that this extra demand will be powered mainly by fossil fuels, when carbon emissions are already at a record high. Research published this week in Nature Sustainability estimates that some 400 data centres in the United States accounted for around 26 megatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, more than those produced by many countries (G. Guidi et al. Nature Sustain. https://doi.org/hcsptc; 2026). And according to a study published last week in Nature Climate Change, data centres’ energy demands could prolong the lifespan of coal-fired power stations (C. Li et al. Nature Clim. Change https://doi.org/rzqr; 2026).

But none of this is inevitable. Governments could mandate that new energy demand be met with renewable sources. And regulators could look at alternative ways to manage existing electric supplies.

Many nations’ electric grid systems are designed to accommodate surges in demand, whether to power extra cooling on hot summer days or extra heating during winter cold snaps. Much of the time, there is excess capacity. This excess could be used to reduce the amount of new energy needed to power data centres.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

One solution is to curtail data-centre operations during periods of peak electricity consumption, and ramp up at times of lower demand. An analysis released in 2025 by researchers at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, found that the US electric grid could accommodate 98 gigawatts of extra demand in this way, without adding any new generation capacity (see go.nature.com/4cdeknm). That 98 gigawatts would be enough to cover most, if not all, of the expected expansion in US data centres over the next few years.

There is potential for this to become a reality. In June, as part of a larger effort to modernize the grid, the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission instructed grid operators to draw up a plan for how they will cope with extra demand from data centres. The technology industry is understandably paying close attention to how it might mitigate the problems of powering data centres. Earlier this month, OpenAI announced what it is calling a “grid protectors program”, a project to consult with US grid operators, regulators and policymakers to see how the company can work around peaks in power demand.

Meanwhile, Google is paying households and businesses in parts of the Eastern United States to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand. Similar proposals are being considered in other countries.

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

These are all tentative moves in the right direction, although arguably progress is not being made fast enough. Policymakers and data-centre operators must engage seriously with those who oppose the centres’ expansion. At a minimum, any new energy sources developed to power these centres must be renewable. Existing energy sources can also be better deployed, and researchers working to develop alternatives to energy-intensive data centres should be better supported. More peer-reviewed evidence is needed, especially for countries outside the United States.

There are smarter and more sustainable ways to power the growth of AI, but to achieve them, concerted and coordinated action will be needed. In this way, the harm posed to people and the planet can be minimized, and AI technologies can benefit everyone.

#714. Sarah Has ‘One Month’ to Leave Her Parents’ Home. She’s 45. (Exclusive Clip, Director Chat)

Writer-director-producer Maya Vitkova-Kosev, known for collaborations with Cristian Mungiu and Radu Jude, discusses her Tallinn premiere in which madness and sadness collide.

Artist Sarah, 45, is in a pickle. With her parents’ 50th wedding anniversary approaching, they give her a shocking ultimatum: After a lifetime of being protected and supported, Sarah has one month to (finally) leave the family home.

The question is: Can Sarah suddenly become independent while navigating dating, reconnecting with ex-boyfriends and complicated feelings about motherhood? Oh yeah, there is also a rather unusual condition her parents mention. If she ever wants to return to living with her parents, she must have a baby – to carry on the family line. Related Stories Movies European Lifetime Achievement Award for the Dardenne Brothers Music Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender Set to Headline Glastonbury 2027

Welcome to the quirky world of One Month, the new feature from Bulgarian writer-director-producer Maya Vitkova-Kosev (Viktoria), who is also known for her collaborations with Cristian Mungiu, Radu Jude and Cristi Puiu. Madness and sadness collide in a very different cinematic experience.

One Month stars Miroslava Gogovska, Mariana Krumova, Marin Yanev, Plamen Velikov and Yordan Rasin. The cinematographer is Krum Rodriguez, with editing by Bernat Aragones.

Ahead of its world premiere in the Critics’ Picks Competition of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia on Wednesday, Vitkova-Kosev talked to THR about her inspiration for One Month during the COVID pandemic, her cast and returning to the mother-daughter relationship.

But first, watch a clip from the film, which THR can exclusively premiere, for a taste of the wackier side of life presented in the film. Warning: you may never dance again!

After watching this wild dance scene, you may wonder how it came together. “Only six or seven of the dancing people are actors. All the rest were extras,” the filmmaker shares. “We knew the piece of music right from the start. And when we started filming, the entire crew was standing at the monitors, laughing. The actors and extras didn’t have any other direction than just to go crazy. So some of them started undressing, as you saw. One of them poured wine over her head. Unfortunately, we had to cut many parts out because otherwise the scene would have become a mastodon in the film.”

No, the premise of the film is not inspired by Vitkova-Kosev’s life! “The idea for the film came totally out of the blue,” she recalls. “It was just a scene that [hit me] at the beginning of the [COVID] pandemic. It was actually one month after we were locked down in Barcelona [where she lives]. I had this idea about a woman who’s been living with her parents forever, and suddenly they have a conversation letting her know that she has a month to go. And I started laughing. Because it was a little bit gloomy at that time, I really needed to entertain myself, so I sat down and wrote it.”

The process of making the film took longer than originally thought, “because I got pregnant, I gave birth, I was breastfeeding my kid, and so on,” the filmmaker quips.

The casting was, of course, key to getting the tonal mix of comedy, drama, loneliness, lack of direction and madness right. Vitkova-Kosev knew Gogovska from an experimental theater group. “I always wanted to do something with her,” she tells THR. “I did a short film a couple of months before we shot One Month, and I invited her. She had a totally different role in the short film, but I wanted to see whether she could bring this sense of humor with a bit of madness, and with drama behind it. And yes, it was clear for me that she was the person.”

You may not recognize the rest of the cast, but some people in Bulgaria still will. “All the older guys are stars, the old stars of Bulgaria,” the director explains. “Some of them had maybe even been forgotten.”

One key theme in Vitkova-Kosev’s new film, and a recurring topic in her work, is a key familial relationship. “This was not an intentional thing,” she tells THR. “But I discovered that it is a mother-daughter story again. In Viktoria, that was intentionally there with three generations of mothers and daughters. Here, I thought this was a totally different thing – I’m just making a funny film.”

In fact, various comedic elements ended up on the cutting-room floor. “Honestly, the film was so much funnier,” Vitkova-Kosev shares. “But my editor Bernat and I aimed to make Sarah’s journey clear. So that meant killing a lot of darlings on the way to make her grow up, to set her free.”

As you can see in the exclusive clip that THR could premiere above, music is a key part of One Month and Sarah’s journey. Among the songs you can hear in the movie are the Bee Gees’ “Stayin’ Alive,” Eagles of Death Metal’s version of George Michael’s “Careless Whisper,” Muse’s “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You” and The Cranberries’ “No Need to Argue.”

“Maybe the hardest thing for this film was getting the music,” Vitkova-Kosev says. “It took me a year and a half. I did it on my own. I didn’t hire anybody to do that. I was in contact with the companies, and the first thing that they had to understand was that we had limitations in the budget. So basically, my choice as a producer was to not pay myself for my work as a screenwriter, director, and producer, but pay for the music. I feel music is important and something that will stay.”

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.

Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole.

However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes.

The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova.

"These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Currently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs.

Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over the past 10 years.

This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also looked at the spin rates of black holes in mergers, a telltale signature of how they formed. This revealed that 10-solar-mass black holes seemed to have a distinct range of spin speeds. This indicates a common origin, perhaps the implosion of a massive star without a supernova explosion.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred concluded. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Physical Review D.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#712. Ron Howard Wasn’t Sure He Was the Right Director for ‘Avedon’; This Is What Changed His Mind

The documentary about famed fashion and portrait photographer Richard Avedon premiered on Netflix on Nov. 11.

Ron Howard knows his way around a camera: in front of and behind the lens; scripted film or documentary feature. But when his production company, Imagine Entertainment (co-chaired by Brian Grazer), was considering a biodoc on fashion photographer Richard Avedon, Howard wasn’t sure if he should be at the helm.

“I really went into it thinking, ‘This is a great subject, it’d be great for Imagine,’” Howard said of the Avedon Foundation opening up the artist’s archives to him during a screening at SCAD Film Festival on Oct. 28. “As I began sort of seeing the breadth of that work, I was immediately impressed, but I still felt like, I’m not sure I’m really the right filmmaker for this, but this is fascinating and I bet we could explore what went on behind the scenes making many of these great photos that we remember.” Related Stories Beyond the Book From Book Club to Netflix: How Katherine Center's 'The Bodyguard' Became 'Guarding Stars' Movies Lee Chang-dong on the Mysteries and Meaning of 'Possible Love'

“As I began to do some research, soon I really did connect with it as this very human story that I wanted to tell,” Howard continued. “It was less anecdotal about how photos were done and what glamorous or intriguing figures sat for him, and much, much more about an artist’s journey, and I related to it. In some ways, we’re very different people — he’s an extrovert, I’m not; he was the life of the party, I avoid them — but, man, did he have drive and ambition.”

The resulting film, Avedon, now streaming on Netflix, blends commentary from collaborators — former magazine editor Tina Brown, model Lauren Hutton and dancer and choreographer Twyla Tharp — with Richard’s works, both commercial and historic, like his portraits of figures of the civil rights movement. The project heavily explores Avedon’s legacy as an artist with strong creative and political convictions, as well as his struggle balancing those passions with his obligations as a husband and father.

“Ultimately, we had 500 photographs in the documentary, but our amazing producing partner, Dallas Brennan Rexer, combed through 16,000 sittings of Avedon,” producer Sara Bernstein, president of Imagine Documentaries, explained during the Q&A. “Initially, we thought there might be a select number of hero images that would take us through Avedon’s creative story. But then there’s this backdrop of, essentially, the back half of the 20th century, so you could match these images with these different moments in history or these different personalities who represent different buckets of history. And then you were able to see a deeper, personal story when John Avedon sat down for us.”

Richard’s son, John, whose son, Michael, is also a fashion photographer, was a “reluctant interview,” despite being supportive of the project, Howard noted as he shared how he got John on board as a talking head.

“Frankly, I said to him, ‘There’s a gap here because we have your father’s voice. We have people who worked with him, but we don’t have that intimate connection, that deeper understanding that’s away from the studio.’ And I think as a writer himself, he recognized that there was a role for him to fill,” said Howard, later adding, “now [the film] became a generational thing about fathers and sons in addition to everything else.”

In one of the final scenes of the film, Avedon, who died in 2001, makes a startlingly reticent prediction about the outlook on his art form, stating, “I don’t think there will be photography in the future, only machines.”

Asked what he thinks Avedon would capture at this moment in time, where the battle between art and AI seems to be reaching its peak, Howard said, “He’d probably still be shooting on the white paper and probably still using that three-by-five camera because, for him, it did become a kind of communication and an exploration, capturing those moments. I think he would still be entirely relevant because he became the story behind the story as an artist. And we began to recognize his work; whether we knew it was Avedon, we could feel the hand of a creator.”

Added Howard of how Richard might approach AI, “My guess is also with his sensibility and aesthetic, he’d be using it as a tool to advance his aesthetic. I don’t think he’d be necessarily running away from it, but he would want to stay in control.”

A simple sound bar can work wonders on a home television setup. It’s for casual music listeners and audiophiles looking for one speaker with built-in subwoofers and an eight-driver array creating a three-dimensional, immersive sound. If this price point is too high, Denon also makes two smaller models, the 200 and the 400.

Turn your living room into a full-fledged home theater with Sony’s Bravia Theater Trio, all you need to create a simple surround-sound experience at home. The three-speaker design works best with large televisions, and the product was created in collaboration with Sony Pictures Entertainment so the sound lives up to the blockbuster standard of today’s filmmakers. We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City."

Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!"

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

Molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

Molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

Revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel."

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

It’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard announced last year in a statement.

"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”
